passage:
I'm Farida, and I still remember the Tuesday I decided my best friend Minakshi hated me. I had asked if she wanted to go to the fair on Sunday. She usually writes things like "yesss!! 😄". This time it said, "Sure." With a full stop. Nothing else.
I read it about ten times. Was the full stop cold? Where was the smiley? I typed "did I do something?" and deleted it, then typed "never mind about the fair" and deleted that too. My hands felt cold.
An hour later Minakshi wrote, "sorry, phone was at 2% and I typed fast! Sunday is perfect 😄". I laughed at myself. The full stop had never meant anything.

qa.q: What did Minakshi reply when asked about the fair on Sunday?
qa.a: Minakshi replied, "Sure." with a full stop and nothing else.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling while rereading "Sure." about ten times?
qa.a: Farida felt anxious and afraid Minakshi was upset. The cold hands and the typed and deleted messages show worry, made worse by the missing smiley.

qa.q: What small step could Farida take next time a reply feels off?
qa.a: Farida could send one calm question, such as asking if everything is okay, and wait for the answer instead of rereading the message. A quick call would work too.

qa.q: What was Minakshi's reason for the short reply?
qa.a: Minakshi's phone was at 2% and Minakshi typed fast, so there was no time for a smiley. The reply came from a low battery, not upset.

grounding: A teenager reads a full stop and missing emoji as a sign that a friend is upset, then learns it was a low phone battery.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Friday. Payal, Class 10, came to my room at lunch with her phone in her hand. She showed me a friend's reply, "fine." and asked, "Isn't that angry? She used to write 'fine!!' with a heart." Payal had not eaten. She said she had rewritten her own message four times.
I asked what else she knew about her friend's week, and Payal said there was a maths test. We talked about how tone is guessed when there is no voice. I suggested she send one open question, and she wrote, "Are we okay? You seemed quiet." Then she ate her lunch. The reply came before the bell: "just tired, come sit with me? 🙂"
Vinita, school counsellor

qa.q: What word did Payal's friend send in the reply she showed the counsellor?
qa.a: The friend's reply said "fine." with a full stop.

qa.q: What might Payal have been worrying about when she rewrote her message four times?
qa.a: Payal was probably anxious that the friend was upset with her. Not eating lunch and rewriting the message show how much the short reply weighed on her.

qa.q: What did Vinita do to help Payal move from guessing to checking?
qa.a: Vinita asked what Payal knew about the friend's week, talked about how tone is guessed in text, and suggested one open question. Payal sent it and got a warm answer.

qa.q: What was the friend probably going through when the reply "fine." was sent?
qa.a: The friend was probably tired, with a maths test that week, and wrote a short word without thinking about tone. The friend then invited Payal to sit together.

grounding: A teenager worries that a full stop in a reply means a friend is upset, and a counsellor helps her ask directly.

passage:
Monday night, Saurabh texted Sarika a picture of the chemistry project model. "What do you think?"
Twenty minutes later: "Looks fine."
Fine, with a full stop. No heart, no thumbs up. Saurabh read it five times. Fine meant bad. The full stop meant she was annoyed. Was it because he'd sat with Karan at lunch? He typed three apologies and deleted them all.
Tuesday, at the lab bench, Sarika was humming and cutting straws for the model. "Your picture was good," she said. "I was helping Nani with the dishes, so I typed fast."
Saurabh laughed, but his shoulders dropped for the first time since the night before.
Two weeks later, his cousin sent "okay." about a family trip. Saurabh felt the old twist in his stomach. He paused. "Am I reading this worried again?" He texted, "Are you in?" The answer came: "Yes!! Sorry, in class."

qa.q: What did Sarika reply to Saurabh's picture?
qa.a: She replied "Looks fine." with a full stop.

qa.q: What was Saurabh worried about on Monday night?
qa.a: Saurabh was anxious that Sarika was annoyed with him, maybe because he'd sat with Karan at lunch, so he felt guilty enough to draft and delete apologies.

qa.q: What small step did Saurabh learn to take?
qa.a: When a message felt cold, he paused, asked himself if he was reading it worried, and then sent a simple question instead of assuming.

qa.q: What was it like for Sarika to send that message?
qa.a: For Sarika it was an ordinary quick reply while helping Nani with the dishes; she was cheerful and had no idea it had caused worry.

grounding: A teenager reads a full stop and no emoji as a friend being upset, and over time learns anxious guesses lean negative.

passage:
"Kunal, I see your face every time someone sends you a message without a smiley," said Tanuja Bua, pulling her chair closer. "Let me tell you about me at fifteen.
"We didn't have chat apps then, only SMS, and each message cost something, so people wrote short. My best friend, Lata, always ended with a smiley made of colon and bracket. One day before our board exams I sent her a long message asking if she was still angry about the seating chart. She sent back one word: 'No.' No smiley.
"I cried in the bathroom. I decided she hated me. For two days I didn't call her.
"Then her mother phoned ours. Lata thought I was avoiding her! Her phone had run out of balance, and she'd sent the shortest thing she could.
"So when you see a full stop, beta, remember what I lost: two days of my best friend, for a missing bracket."

qa.q: What did Lata send back to Tanuja Bua's long message?
qa.a: Lata sent back one word, "No.", with no smiley.

qa.q: How did Tanuja Bua feel as a fifteen-year-old when she read the reply?
qa.a: She felt hurt and afraid that Lata hated her, crying in the bathroom and avoiding her for two days.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what could young Tanuja have done instead?
qa.a: The turning point was Lata's mother phoning; young Tanuja could have called Lata that same day to ask, instead of staying silent for two days.

qa.q: How did Lata experience those two days?
qa.a: Lata felt confused and hurt, thinking Tanuja was avoiding her, since she had only sent a short reply because her phone ran out of balance.

grounding: An elder recalls a teenage worry over a missing smiley, showing tone in text is guessed and leans negative when anxious.

passage:
It was exam week in the hostel, the lights had gone out, and Hrithik had eleven percent battery. He was saving it for the torch and the chemistry notes, but he sent one message to Ujjwal in the next wing: "Can I borrow your formula sheet tomorrow?"
Ujjwal usually replied with a grin emoji and three exclamation marks. This time: "ok."
Hrithik stared at the dot. Maybe Ujjwal was fed up with lending him things. Maybe he thought Hrithik never prepared. In the dark, with battery dropping, every guess got worse. He almost typed "forget it" but stopped. The phone showed eight percent.
He walked down the corridor with the torch instead. Ujjwal was sitting on his bed with a candle, the sheet already on top of his pile.
"Here. Sorry, I was typing with one thumb, holding the candle with the other."
Hrithik laughed so hard the candle flickered.

qa.q: How much battery did Hrithik have when the lights went out?
qa.a: Hrithik had eleven percent battery.

qa.q: What was Hrithik worried about when he saw "ok."?
qa.a: Hrithik was anxious that Ujjwal was fed up with lending him things or thought he never prepared, and the dark and stress made each guess feel worse.

qa.q: What choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Instead of sending "forget it", Hrithik walked down the corridor to see Ujjwal, which cleared the worry in seconds.

qa.q: What would change if Hrithik had sent "forget it"?
qa.a: Ujjwal would likely feel confused and hurt, since he had already put the sheet on his pile, and a small misreading could have turned into a real quarrel.

grounding: A teenager worries that a full stop and missing emoji mean a friend is upset, and exam stress makes the guesses lean negative.

passage: On the Pune bus home, Zainab sent Arohi a photo of the poster she had finished for the science fair, with a sparkle ✨. The reply came four minutes later: "Looks good." A full stop. No sparkle, no heart. Zainab stared. Arohi always sent hearts. Was it the poster? Or that Zainab had sat with Kavya at lunch? She scrolled up through a week of messages, hunting for clues, and counted: fewer emojis since Monday. Her stomach knotted. At home she typed "r u mad at me?", deleted it, typed it again, and finally sent it. Arohi replied in seconds: "what?? no 😅 was in the dentist chair, typing w one hand. poster is actually SO good ❤️" Zainab laughed out loud, then noticed her shoulders had been up by her ears the whole ride.

qa.q: Where was Arohi when she sent "Looks good."?
qa.a: Arohi was in the dentist chair.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling as she scrolled back through a week of messages?
qa.a: Zainab felt anxious and insecure, with a knotted stomach, reading worry into a full stop and fewer emojis.

qa.q: Which choice finally ended Zainab's worry, and what could she do sooner next time?
qa.a: Asking directly, "r u mad at me?", got the real answer in seconds; next time she could ask straight away instead of hunting for clues.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel on seeing "r u mad at me?"
qa.a: Arohi would likely be surprised, since her short reply meant nothing and she actually loved the poster, and keen to reassure Zainab quickly.

grounding: Shows a teenager who reads a full stop and a missing emoji as a friend being upset, and whose anxious guess turns out wrong.
